Just in order
that the chronology of these historic events may be accurately recorded, my right hon. friend in opening his remarks this afternoon said that this was the first Imperial conference that had been held in Canada. I assume he meant the first Imperial economic conference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Colonial conferences came later to be known, as Imperial conferences. This -is the first imperial economic conference to be held in this Dominion. In speaking some days ago on the
2782	COMMONS
Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
budget, my right hon. friend conveyed the impression that this conference had no connection with that of 1930; that it was not the postponed conference agreed to at the time. By his words as reported in Hansard, I think he rather left the impression that this conference was something which was due wholly to himself, and one that had been arranged for the first time as a result, in part, of the recent elections in Great Britain. In case I may be doing my right hon. friend an injustice in misstating his position, I should like to read exactly what he said. The words will be found in Hansard, page 2406 of April 26 of this year. My right hon. friend, referring to the Imperial economic conference to be held here this year made this statement:
It is said by him-[DOT]
That was of myself.
-to be regarded as the adjournment of the former conference. I believe it is not so regarded; at least I am so informed. It may be that the conference of 1930 was a failure. The right hon. gentleman said it has been described by someone as a tragedy.
The point I wish to bring out at the present
moment is that the statement I have just read would certainly lead us to believe that this conference was not the postponed conference of 1930.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Neither it is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: My right hon. friend says "neither it is." I confess I am at a loss to understand his view, and I do not know what members of delegations from other parts of the empire will feel when they see that statement, because my right hon. rriend was very emphatic at the Imperial conference of 1930 in stating that he would like the economic conference to be postponed, to meet in Ottawa later on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Again may I
read his exact words. In his opening address which appears under the heading "Statement by the Prime Minister of Canada," the Prime Minister put forward proposals which, as he has since told us, he thought would be rejected. He said he put them forward deliberately expecting that they would be rejected. That will come rather as a surprise to members of that conference. My right hon. friend went on to suggest the basis upon which a conference might be held, and he concluded with these words: I am reading from the report of the Imperial Conference of 1930, English edition, page 34:

Consistent with the fullest inquiry into the application pf the principle of an empire preference, our deliberations must be governed by the time factor. If this change in our economic relationship is to be made, it must be made without undue delay. I would therefore, propose that this conference, if it approve the principle should constitute such committee as may, with the greatest expedition and thoroughness, consider the various questions incident to its operation. As we have here neither the time, nor the machinery necessary, to reach a final conclusion upon all of them, it is apparent that we must employ the technicians of our respective countries to complete the inquiry. And for that purpose I would suggest that committees be set up in each of the countries concerned; and that these committees commence immediately an exhaustive examination of the effect upon their domestic situation of the proposals I have made.
Then, under the subheading "Suggested conference at Ottawa," the report continues:
I am satisfied that whatever modifications in the general plan Canada may have to suggest wall be ready for submission within a period of six months. I assume that you are all capable of a like measure of expedition, and so I further propose that, when this economic conference has had an opportunity profitably to discuss the plan in its various aspects, it do adjourn to meet at Ottawa early next year, as the guests of the Canadian people, and that in the interval, through the instrumentalities I have suggested, full and final reports be prepared for submission to it.
In his concluding speech on November 14, as reported at page 225 my right hon. friend spoke as follows:
I would therefore move the adjournment of the economic section of this conference to Ottawa to meet upon a date within the next twelve months to be agreed upon, and I wish, on behalf of the Canadian people, to assure you of their most hearty welcome.
And concluding he said:
I therefore move, Mr. Chairman, that the economic section of the conference adjourn to Ottawqa to meet within the next twelve months at a date to be mutually agreed upon.
I have always understood, and I am sure that all the delegates who were present at the Imperial conference understood, that that was the resolution that was adopted and the plan that was intended.
May I recall to my right hon. friend's mind the fact that we were told last year that unfortunately the postponed conference which was then to have met, had to be again postponed because of the inability of certain other parts of the empire to be represented, but it was always the postponed conference to which reference was made, and certainly until my right hon. friend made the statement two days ago, to which I have just drawn attention, everyone, in all parts of the empire, had the impression that the conference

Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
now about to be held was the postponed economic conference of 1930. I am a little at a loss to understand why my right hon. friend should not so regard it unless it is that another remark which he made in the course of his address helps to throw light upon it.
My right hon. friend told us that he himself had been the first to suggest an economic conference, that he had done so in 1928, that it had been the ambition of his life to see that such a conference was held if he ever came into power. I do not want to take away from my right hon. friend any honour to which he may be entitled, but I would remind him that there was an Imperial economic conference held in 'Great Britain in 1923 as well as an Imperial conference, and that the Imperial economic conference was attended by representatives of the government of Canada as well of the other dominions. The late Sir Lomer Gouin and the Right Hon. George P. Graham were two of Canada's representatives at the Imperial economic conference held in 1923. That was I believe the first Imperial economic conference. It is true that in speaking on the address in 1929 my right hon. friend did say that he thought we should have an economic conference in Canada, but in the course of his remarks what he stressed was not what he has been mentioning to us this afternoon as all-important for the purposes of the conference, the questions of currency and trade. He spoke then more particularly of development and settlement. That was the object of the conference my right hon. friend had in his mind. I have his remarks in that connection here. Speaking on February 11, 1929, the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, said as reported at page 28 of Hansard of that date:
There are two great problems that confront the people of the British Empire; they are the largest problems that have ever been offered for the solution of men and women in any age.
Then he goes on to speak of the size of the British Empire, and so forth, and after having noted its resources and their extent he continued:
So I suggest to the government that since England can no longer take the lead with respect to this matter, this country should call a great economic conference to meet in Ottawa. Let the Dominion of Canada take the lead; let us call an economic conference of the British Empire to meet in this city to consider, after being properly informed, the two great problems of settlement and development.
That was the conference my right hon. friend had in mind, that was the ambition of his life at that time, and yet to-day he does not mention at all the words "settlement
and development" in stating to the house the subjects that are to ibe those of first consideration at this conference. So clearly this conference cannot have any relation to the conference that my right hon. friend had in mind in 1929 if we are to judge by the remarks that he then made. My right hon. friend went on to say:
I can only say that if we who sit to the left of the Speaker were entrusted with the responsibilities of power to-morrow one of our first actions would be to ask that representatives of this great empire meet in this capital city of Ottawa in a great economic conference to grapple and deal with the problems of settlement and development, for one-fourth of the world's people are not trustees for nothing. Where England may not take the lead, as she may not at the moment in a matter of this kind for reasons which are obvious, we may point the way, remembering that the first of the colonial conferences, which ultimately became imperial conferences, sat in this city.
A great economic conference brought together through the initiative of the Canadian government would be able to work out a solution of these problems which would not be temporary in its character, which would not be subject to adverse and hostile legislation, but which would represent the agreed views of one-fourth of the world's pdople, occupying one-fourth of the world's area. That in itself would do much to secure for all time that outlawry of war, that perpetual peace, for which all democracies are striving.
That was the kind of conference my right hon. friend had in mind in 1929, and I think we still have vivid recollections of the elaborate scheme of settlement which was proposed by the present Senator McRae, at that time a member of this house, and which seemed at the time to bear a very close relationship to what my right hon. friend had in view when he was speaking of an economic conference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: It synchronized.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Yes, as my
colleague suggests, it seemed to synchronize with the statement of my right hon. friend's views. I hope that the Prime Minister will tell us whether this important question of settlement, which means, of course, migration from different parts of the empire to other parts, is to be one of the main subjects of consideration at the coming conference, and what the policy of the government of Canada will be with respect thereto; also, perhaps my right hon. friend will tell us what is meant by development in connection with the policy that he suggested in 1929. I might add that the Liberal administration of the day did extend in 1929, invitations to Great Britain and other self-governing parts of the empire for an economic conference to be held in
2784	COMMONS
Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
Canada, if possible, during 1930. My right hon. friend said that we took the idea from him. Frankly I do not wish to say that we were not as indebted to him as he might be to us for an exchange of views now and then, but the kind of economic conference that we had in view was one which related to trade more particularly than to anything else, and it had not as one of its specific subjects for consideration the question of settlement, which was one of the two main questions in my right hon. friend's mind at the time he spoke in 1929. I might say to my right hon. friend that if he -will speak with those who were at the Imperial conference in Great Britain in 1926, he will discover that the point of view which, as representing Canada, I myself, put forward with respect to conferences was that Imperial conferences dealing with political questions might be held from time to time in London, although I doubted the wisdom of too great frequency of conferences of that kind, and that subsidiary conferences dealing with economic questions might with advantage be held from time to time in different parts of the empire. For instance, that there might be a conference on communications within the empire, held, say, in Australia one year; that a conference with respect to some other economic phase might meet in another part of the empire; that a conference, for example, for increasing the facilities and opportunities for trade within the empire might be made the subject of a separate conference, and that was the conference we suggested in 1929 should be held in Ottawa, trade being considered by us the most important question. The elections came on in the summer of 1930. I think the economic conference was postponed, or rather fixed for London, in view of the decision of the British government after conference with other parts of the empire to hold an economic conference, as well as an Imperial political conference-if I may so describe it-simultaneously in London some time during the year 1930. Speaking on the budget in May, 1930, my right hon. friend made further reference to the conference to which he had previously referred. At page 1827, after quoting his remarks of the previous year, Hansard contains the following statement:
I then concluded with the suggestion that representatives of this great empire should meet in Ottawa and deal with the problems of settlement and development, because one-fourth of the world's people are not trustees for nothing. I repeat that it is desirable and necessary that there should be a conference of representatives from every part of this empire, 
and that conference cannot be held successfully in Great Britain. That is the position which I would expect to be taken by a government having the interests of the empire at heart. But this government is following its old policy; there never has been a time when the Liberal party was not prepared to gamble with Canada and with the British Empire.
I think that makes quite clear my contention as to the nature of the conference my right hon. friend had in mind. There is a paragraph preceding the one I have read which might be read to reinforce my statement:
Well, I have in my hand a return brought down the other day, and I observe that the Prime Minister of our country

Referring to me-
-sent an invitation for an economic conference in Canada sometime after I had on the speech from the throne suggested that there were two great problems with which the British Empire was concerned, the one fiscal and the other the migration of peoples, and that the only method by which these matters could be satisfactorily dealt with was by having a great economic conference here in Ottawa.
It is just as well to have the record complete. The fact is that the first Imperial economic conference was held in London in 1923, and was attended by representatives from Canada and other parts of the empire. In 1929 my right hon. friend suggested an economic conference to be held in Ottawa to deal primarily with questions of settlement and development. In the same year, after my right hon. friend's speech-but not because of it, but rather in accordance with a suggestion which had been made at the conference in Great Britain in 1926-the Liberal government of the day did extend an invitation to other parts of the empire for an economic conference to be held at Ottawa in the following year to deal with trade questions. After that invitation had been sent, my right hon. friend repeated his desire for a conference which among other things would deal primarily with the fiscal question and that of migration. In the fall of 1930 the Imperial conference of 1930 was held in London, and so far as the economic side of it was concerned was a tragedy or a farce. It was postponed on the suggestion of the present Prime Minister for a period of about six months. When that time had expired it had again to be postponed to this year because other parts of the empire could not be represented. There is no gainsaying that the coming conference is simply a postponed edition of the conference of 1930. I do not wonder however that my right hon. friend wants to get as far away as possible from the conference of 1930. If he will boldly throw overboard the proposals he made at that conference, all of us

Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
would be glad to have the line of separation as marked as possible. At the moment I should like my right hon. friend to indicate whether the subject of migration or settlement is to be one of the questions at the coming conference, and if so what will be the view or policy of the administration as put forth at the conference in respect thereto.

I am quite content. I am not at all concerned in whose brain cell the thought originated which subsequently blossomed into an act. I am not concerned with that; it is not a matter which gives me the least thought at the moment.
He then points out that this must be an adjourned conference. I ventured to suggest the other evening that I believed it was not so regarded, and I find that I am right. The reason was this: When the former conference was held in 1930 it was suggested by me, in the course of the few observations I made at the opening, that a period not exceeding six months should elapse during which an opportunity might be afforded for considering questions which were at the basis of any discussions which would result in concrete action. That was not accomplished, and at the end of the conference I moved it be adjourned, to be held within twelve months. Within twelve months it was not held, and when there was an election in Great Britain I sent invitations by cable asking if it were possible to have a new economic conference convened here. Whether or not it was to be regarded as an adjournment did not at that particular moment cross my mind. I had not thought about it in that sense,
and I cannot say that the matter gave me any cause for thought until the right hon. gentleman raised the point the other evening. Most Canadians-with the exception of the right hon. leader of the opposition-will be glad enough to have the conference in Ottawa, postponed or otherwise. In this strange desire that manifests itself in such peculiar ways that nothing shall happen unless he "happens" it, that nothing shall transpire unless he is behind the movement-that obsession that seizes him and has been apparent all through his public life, and never more than this afternoon-he says this is an adjourned conference. What difference does it make?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
What difference does it
make? Does any hon. member see any difference between an adjourned conference and any other kind? Lest it should be thought that the government, in sending out an invitation to a conference to be held here in July next, should derive in the minds of the Canadian electorate any credit for having conceived or suggested the conference, he must say: "This is an adjourned conference; there is nothing about it for which this government can get credit. I sent an invitation in 1929 which was not accepted." Mr Chairman, surely we have got beyond that. Surely we have got beyond a debating school. Surely we have got beyond the idea held by the college student who says, "I, with my little bow and arrow-I shot cock robin." Surely we are past that stage. But no; the right hon. leader of the opposition is intent upon that.
That is the explanation of the discussion with respect to the postponed conference. So far as I can recall, the word "postponed" with respect to the conference has not been used in any communication which has passed, and the governments of the various sections of the empire, if one may judge by the responses they have sent to the invitations forwarded, have treated it as a conference convened by the Dominion of Canada. I had not thought of it in the sense of claiming any merit. I merely treat this government as being an instrument to bring about a gathering of the representatives of the British empire for the purpose of discussing matters which I believe to be of the utmost interest not only to the empire but to the peace of the world.
Now, in 1929 I made the observations to which the hon. gentleman referred, and I also ventured to call attention to the resources of this country and of other countries that comprise the British empire-nickel, asbestos, timber, and the other great natural
2786	COMMONS
Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
resources such as there are throughout every part of the world, in practically every zone, we have within the empire. I developed the idea that if we had thought more of that and less of other countries we might have had greater stability of trade, and I mentioned the two headings under which it seemed to me we might fairly consider our position-settlement and development. The problem of settlement I pointed out arose because in certain parts of this great empire there are areas in which you have congested population, while in others you have great open spaces in which you require population. I realize that the economic crisis through which the world is passing has made discussion of settlement a matter of extreme difficulty. When the right hon. gentleman asks whether it will ibe discussed or not, I can only say that individuals have suggested that the matter of migration might readily be discussed; not that there is any likelihood of migration of people from one part of the empire to the other at this moment, but that the whole subject might reasonably be discussed, not in detail, but looking to the future rather than to the present with improved conditions that must result if time is to bring about the changes which we believe it will. Under those circumstances doubtless the question of migration would be suggested for discussion. But it has not been placed upon any agenda or paper that has been circulated up to the moment beyond inquiries as to whether or not in the view of some, having regard to what has been suggested by others, the matter should be considered. Beyond that I cannot say. But any thoughtful man who looks into the future, who visualizes fifty years hence and considers what the position is in Great Britain with its population, must realize the one fact that is outstanding in this country, that if we are to survive in the end we must have more population. Every thoughtful man knows that at the moment economic conditions make it our business to see to it that we do what we can to prevent unemployment or lack of opportunity for employment becoming more acute by reason of bringing additional people into this country. We have pointed that out. There come crises in the history of all nations, and at the moment we have a crisis during which it is not desirable to add to our population. But you have great congested areas of the British empire. The people there should, it seems to me, if one looks to the future half a century hence, find opportunity for development in other parts of that empire that their ancestors, as well as those who now live within the immediate territory affected, won for them 
and for all who might come after. In those spheres of thinly settled communities there are opportunities for those who come from the congested areas to find and make for themselves homes. That is what I mentioned with respect to the question of settlement and development.
Now, I am willing to submit to any impartial tribunal of my fellow-citizens if they think it is worth considering as constructive criticism on the part of the leader of a great party who has been Prime Minister to try to imply that development does not mean trade. Would any thoughful man say that? Would any one who is not actuated by some motives that prevent him from seeing the real situation not realize that development and trade mean exactly the same thing? I had been pointing out in this instance as I did in others the fact-and I cited from Hansard that in this empire we had vast deposits of nickel, asbestos and other raw materials, and I said:
I will not at this time endeavour to point out what the resources of this empire are, nor how great a part Canada plays in any development of these resources. In nickel, asbestos, lead, tin, gold, silver, metals, minerals, wood products-in all these there are abundant resources in Canada as well as in other parts of the empire: copper in Rhodesia, diamonds in South Africa and great cotton fields in India and Egypt. We have one-fourth of the people of the world, although it is true that part of them are backward races unsuited to our country. So I suggest to the government that since England can no longer take the lead with respect to. this matter, this country should call a great economic conference to meet in Ottawa. Let the Dominion of Canada take the lead.
I was pointing out the basis of all trade. I had referred to our vast and fertile plains, to our great and varied resources, and I had pointed out they were not in one part of the empire, but in Rhodesia, India and other parts of the world. Surely if development means anything it means trade; and trade means development-the development of our resources. I believe this economic conference that is to meet here in July must sit down and consider the question of the development of the resources of the empire. I have pointed out so often that I will not repeat in this house that these great resources are held in trust by the crown for all the people who are within the empire, meaning not only the people of to-day but the people of to-morrow. I ventured then to point out that the toil and the sacrifice and the struggle of men and women in days long since gone by had won these for this population. I believe that still. As I have said, these resources scattered all over the world are held in trust by the crown -the common symbol of a common holding

Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
in trust for all the people of the commonwealth of nations that comprise the empire.
The problem is the development of those resources. That involves in the largest sense the trade of peoples, whether or not, for instance, the requirements with respect to nickel in one part of the empire might be met by the resources of Canada, and the requirements of Canada with respect to other raw materials might be well met by drawing upon the resources of some other part of the empire. In other words, reciprocity in empire products and in empire trade I believe would be very valuable and beneficial. I have ever endeavoured in this house and elsewhere to advocate reciprocity in empire trade, pointing out that I believe if we could serve the interests of one part by reciprocally improving its conditions we were doing a very great service to the whole. I will not dwell upon these matters. I shall leave it to the judgment of this committee as to whether or not the question of development in the sense in which it was used by me with the surrounding context did not involve in the largest and truest sense development of trade in every part of the empire. I am not unmindful of the fact that mistakes may always be made, and they always are made. I certainly am one of those who believe that the only crime you can attribute to a public man is that he remains ignorant despite the warnings of age and experience. Opportunity is afforded to all of us to add to the sum total of our knowledge, and I have never been one of those who are not prepared to admit error-

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
-who are not prepared
to admit error for the purpose of indicating that I have secured benefits by reason of age and experience. But there are certain principles which endure, and the principles to which in my youth I adhered, and which I still believe in, are that we have in this great commonwealth-not by accident-the greatest estate that Providence ever gave to a people; I believe we are accountable for the development of that estate, and the manner in which we have developed and are developing it will be the measure of our sense of obligation and realization of our own trusteeship. If the government, in its endeavour to bring about such a meeting in this city, has had in mind one object more than any other it has been that the men and women-because women on the outside will do much to influence the opinions of men within, as they always have- who meet here as representatives of this vast commonwealth, will endeavour to the best of
their ability to devise policies whereby mutual benefits may come with advantage to the whole, that we may, in vigour and strength, maintain that commonwealth which, I am as convinced as I can be of anything in this world, means more for the preservation of the liberty and freedom of mankind than any other secular institution the world has erected. That is my position.
If you ask as to our policies with respect to the conference I can only say that other governments as well as this realize that this is not a mere meeting together of men for the purpose of dealing with the material things of life. There are other forces that must be reckoned with; there are other values that must be determined, and that very fact operates in men's minds, governs their actions, restrains their conduct and disciplines their observations. Any thoughtful suggestions that may come as to how these ends might be best accomplished will be welcomed, but carping criticism, cynicism and endeavours to make it appear that one's views in 1929 with regard to development and settlement do not agree with one's views in 1932 with regard to the advancement of trade and the improvement of economic conditions, are neither helpful nor constructive. This is merely elemental cynicism disguised as a form of what might be called elementary criticism.
That is the position, and if we seek assistance by suggestion it does not mean for a single moment that we do not realize that there is a body of public opinion that is not represented by observations such as those to which we have just listened. There are thoughtful men and women in this country belonging to the Liberal party who are every day making timely suggestions as to how we can best make a success of this gathering. They are not thinking in terms of party; they are not concerned with whether or not there is a Conservative government or a Liberal government in power at the moment. What they are concerned with is that there shall be the very greatest effort made, at this great moment in the history of the world, this time of its greatest crisis, on the part of representative men from every part of a quarter of its area, to evolve policies and formulate plans for the future that will ensure peace, happiness and prosperity to the peoples they represent and, by mutual concession and expressions of good will with respect to trade and the development of the resources of this estate of ours, that we may be able to attain that end. Despite all that may be said and all the unfair allusions that may be made by
2788	COMMONS
Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
the Liberal party, its chiefs and its lieutenants, on the public platform or in this house, we will endeavour to the best of our ability to discharge the responsibility that the Canadian people have imposed upon us, and advance reciprocal benefits, if we can, to every part of this empire in order to ensure the harmonious development of the whole and the peace and prosperity of all its peoples.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I shall not
endeavour to follow my right hon. friend in the vituperative strain he has thought it advisable to adopt, not only towards myself but towards the Liberal party as a whole. One would have thought that at a moment such as this he above all others would have endeavoured to disclose, by his words and his manner generally, a desire for cooperation in connection with a great imperial undertaking such as that *which is about to take place. Fortunately my right hon. friend will be judged bj' his own words and acts, and I am quite prepared to leave any judgment respecting him to that record.
What I do think is important in a matter of this kind is that there should be historical accuracy in regard to all matters, and certainly those matters which affect other parts of the British Empire as well as Canada. My previous references were made wholly with the view of placing on Hansard an accurate historical statement of the developments which led to the present conference. I thought I did my -right hon. friend a kindness by quoting his own words, but I see I have done him an unkindness; I see there is nothing that strikes him quite so hard as his own utterances when they are brought back to him. I spared him, in the first remarks I made, any quotation from that part of Hansard where he sought to claim the entire credit for this conference. I had no motive so petty as that of comparison between my right hon. friend and myself; I am sure he is welcome to any superior position he may wish to assume. I only desired to maintain an accurate historical record, particularly when my right hon. friend sought to take away from one who was a really great man in the leadership of affairs in this country some credit that attaches to him in matters of imperial affairs. I will read from page 2408 of Hansard for this year so that the house may see for itself whether I was claiming credit for all that was done; who, in fact, the "I" was who made the claim:
Mr. Bennett: Well, if they are interested in reading Hansard they will find that as long ago as 1928-

I think that should have been 1929.
-I had said -that if we had power my first effort would be to endeavour to call an economic conference of the British empire in this city. I went to London with a very definite idea in my mind. I gave expression to it, and I believed it would be received exactly as it was received. But I said there was a principle that had to be settled first. Those who will do me the honour of reading what I said wil-l find clearly stated the principle that must first be settled. The electors of Great Britain settled it. As soon as they had settled it I invited the representatives of every part of the British empire to come to this city to a conference, and the date has been fixed for the 21st day of July. They are coming, so they say. Therefore the purpose which I had in mind in 1928, which I never failed to keep before me, the one ambition that I entertained if we did come to power I hoped to see realized. In that regard may I say that I have under my hand the memorandum left by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1902, when he ceased to agree with his colleagues and took a definite stand with respect to Imperial preference. It is true it was not followed by action, it is true it was not followed by any considered effort to achieve it, but when T read it it will be realized that we at least have now seen accomplished that which he said should be accomplished but failed to accomplish, as did his successors in office.
I leave it to hon. members of the house whether my right hon. friend's own words do *not speak more eloquently than it would be *possible for any individual to do, as to who is *claiming undue credit and seeking to take away from others credit which is their due.

At the risk of drawing
upon myself another lecture from the right hon. gentleman, I desire to venture a few words. In the first place I am glad that the right hon. gentleman seems to consider this coming conference as a new venture, altogether free from any impediments which the conference of 1930 might have placed in the way. My right hon. friend seems to have modified his views to some extent, though he will not admit it. He spoke of Viscount Snowden's interpretation of his words in view of the context of the speech in which he made the proposal which I indicated a few moments ago. I happen to have the words of Viscount Snowden, uttered after that offer had been made by my right hon. friend, and he certainly interpreted the proposal exactly as it was made. Speaking at Manchester some time afterwards, Viscount Snowden made two definite pronouncements about his own and his government's views regarding tariffs. I quote from the Manchester Guardian:
It had been reported, he said, that the government was considering the imposition of an allround 10 per cent import duty for revenue purposes. "No government in which I am in charge of the national finances will ever give serious consideration to a proposal like that."

Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
Again, referring to the government as a whole: "We said we were anxious to do everything practicable to foster and encourage our imperial trade, but we would not support any proposal which involved the taxation of food, raw materials, or a general protectionist policy. That still remains the attitude of the government."
I quote that merely to show what Viscount Snowden thought of the proposal then made. Whether he was right or wrong, he obviously viewed the offer of my right hon. friend in the same way as I indicated it this afternoon.

He must have changed
his mind since.

I am not sure about that;
I do not think he has changed his mind. My hon. friends are wrong altogether in their view of what has happened in England. They think that England has become protectionist for all time. That is not true. It is merely an expedient, as they know, so much so that the members of that so-called National government in England are speaking against protection at the present time. I read only a few days ago a violent and bitter indictment of protection by Sir Herbert Samuel, who is one of the leading ministers in that government.
Of course, this is a time when all things happen. We are living in an abnormal period in the history of the world and it seems rather strange that these things should happen. But it shows that protection as a permanent policy has not yet been accepted by England. They had a doctor's mandate, apparently, but they agreed to disagree on many things, and this is one of them. I could quote views of Sir Herbert Samuel with regard to an economic unit in the British Commonwealth of Nations, and those views certainly are in harmony with the views I hold personally.
So far as this coming conference is concerned-and I am not criticizing the policy of the government if I modestly suggest some things regarding it-my right hon. friend says that there is no policy. He is inviting suggestions, though the way he answers them is not very pleasant to those who offer the suggestions. May I suggest to my right hon. friend that perhaps he is wrong when he tries to imitate his High Commissioner in London by disparaging the mental equipment ol those who do not agree with him.

the high commissioner, who thinks that all those who do not agree with him are of short vision or low calibre or something of that kind. However, this conference, to be at all successful, must proceed, I submit, along the lines of lowering the tariff. It would be impossible to come to any understanding and to any successful conclusion by adhering to the policies as expressed by my right hon. friend at the conference of 1930. There is emerging from the present depression something that justifies the saying that it is an ill wind-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: An ill wind that blows nobody good.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Yes, an ill wind that blows nobody good; because many people have begun to realize that this race of high tariffs which is being entered into everywhere is a mad race. The idea that the foreigner is a person who must buy but never sell has unfortunately spread from Bedlam to every capital of the world. People are realizing to-day that it is a mistake, in view of the results that are so apparent. The international trade of the world is at a standstill. We have been erecting barriers everywhere. My right hon. friend's proposal in 1930, that we should not lower our tariff at all but that we should raise it ten per cent higher, except for exempting Great Britain and the other dominions from that ten per cent, was certainly not a fair offer, if I may use a mild expression, to make the sister nations of the commonwealth. What benefit will England obtain if she cannot get through Canada's door? What benefit will she obtain because foreign countries are still ten per cent further from our door than she is? And that is exactly the proposal that was made. Indeed, what benefit could we derive ourselves?
I agree with my right hon. friend in what he said this afternoon, that this should be a negotiation based on mutual advantages. I prefer that to the word sacrifices. If you try to base the maintenance of the British Commonwealth of Nations on sacrifices, you are inviting something which at some time or other may be dangerous. What is better is mutual benefit, and no fixed bargaining, nothing that would be a fetter instead of a tie. The union of the British nations must rest upon perfect and absolute freedom. I do not like the term economic unit, which was used this afternoon by one of the speakers on the resolution of my hon. friend from Acadia. An economic union of the empire would mean an economic group against the rest of the world. Let us try to have larger and freer trade as between the nations of
2790	COMMONS
Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
the empire. But we must remain free and autonomous in our economic policies as well as in our other policies, for that is the only way to remain friends and brothers. Mr. Chairman, there is nothing so dangerous, as you know, as business matters and business difficulties between members of a family; they are much more serious and much graver than friction between strangers in business affairs. Our understanding, if there is one- and I hope there will be-must be absolutely founded rather on a gentleman's agreement, a friendly entente as between ourselves, than on any strict rule and bargaining based merely on self interest. I, if I may use the first personal pronoun in a modest way, have always held those views. But I am pleased that I am not alone; I have been sharing them with others. They were those of Mr. Asquith, of Lord Grey. If I had time-and unfortunately I cannot be present to-night-I could quote expressions of opinion of many people, but even at the present time the leading economists and writers in the empire reviews are alluding to the very danger which I have been suggesting. I have in my hand the last edition of the Spectator, of April 30, 1932, and it indicates exactly what I have just been saying about the danger which is ahead. Let me quote only a sentence:
If one of the delegates at Ottawa, thinking to do his duty by those who sent him, tries to get the better of another delegate, the rift in the family is opened. No doubt we should love our butcher and our baker as ourselves, but a still prior duty is to love the brotherhood or sisterhood, and we may be sure that those who do not first show love in the family do not show it in "business." And, if bargains must be, there is danger of forgetting that the best bargain is never the one by which you or I gain, but that by which we both gain.
My last word is that I think we must see to it that the empire does not stand or fall on or because of the tariff. Our idea of union between the British nations must not be based on tariffs, on duties, or even on preferences.

It is generally recognized that such a procedure is wrong, and while temporary relief might be afforded by a bonus it could not ultimately redound to the advantage of agriculture or of the country in general. Of course we know that these estimates are not sanctioned simply by the
Minister of Agriculture himself, but represent the joint conclusion of the whole cabinet, and undoubtedly the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have set the seal of their approval on the reductions that have been made. But I repeat it does seem strange that at this time, when agriculture is at such a low ebb that everything that can possibly be done to assist it should be done,-these estimates should be cut so drastically. There may be some places where economies would be desirable. There may have been expenditures in the past in certain directions that were not fully justified. I think the hon. member for Weyburn and myself will heartily approve of the action of the minister and the government in cutting out the grant to the National Dairy Council. speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman, all hon. members realize that perhaps from the standpoint of agriculture no country in the world has so many difficult problems. The fact that we have about six hundred thousand farmers scattered over an area so extensive from east to west and from north to south, operating under a wide range of climatic conditions and producing a variety of farm products, give rise to many difficult problems. For instance, due to climatic conditions alone it is necessary for us to give careful study to ascertain what breeds of cattle are best suited to the different sections of the country. We have also had to carry on extensive investigations, more extensive than those carried on in any other country, in, order to develop grass, grain and other seeds best suited to our varying climatic conditions. Then again our fruit farmers labour under a great handicap because along four thousand miles of boundary line their competitors in the United States have a decided advantage over them with respect to climate, for fruit and vegetables can be produced earlier in the 
United States and they come on our market at a time when our fruit and vegetable growers feel the competition very injurious to their interests. That in itself has always been a very difficult problem for our agriculturists.
But difficult as it was, in 1929, due to the fact that the tariff barriers had been raised so high against the entry of our farm products into the United1 States, we found ourselves confronted with another problem that was almost more difficult to solve than those which we had already overcome; I refer to the problem of marketing. Much has been said about production, and for years the United States tariff was such that it was possible for our farmers to market their products to advantage along the boundary line. In fact, it was as though our farmers had an extended domestic market in the United States. One of the results of the proximity of the large cities to the south, where ou-r farmers could market their products, was to give direction to the kind of products they produced. But with the raising of the tariff wall, shutting out our goods from the United States, we were confronted with an entirely new question, the question of marketing our farm products through our eastern and western gateways. No preparation had been made to meet that contingency by any previous government because it had not been necessary, due to the reasons that I have fairly set forth. Therefore we are now confronted with a problem even more difficult than that of diversified production-the problem of marketing. To this problem I have perhaps given more attention than to any other in connection with agriculture since I took this portfolio.
Irrespective of party affiliations, we must meet fairly this question: What can we, as agriculturists, produce to the best advantage to compete with similar products on the European market? Because that is practically the only market that is left to us, particularly the market of the United Kingdom. To decide that question we must take into consideration many different factors or elements. First, we have to consider the long freight haul, whether rail or steamship. Then due to our short summers and long winters the cost of certain types of farming is very much increased and seriously handicaps our farmers in competing on the world's market with the farmers of other nations who do not labour under such handicaps. We must also take into consideration the products that we can produce in sufficient quantities so that once we obtain a foothold on the world's market -the British market-we can ensure a uniform continuity of supply of such high quality as

Supply-A griculture
will enable us to compete with the products of other countries. Another very important question is the cost of production. Not the least question is the standard of living of the farmers who are putting their goods on the world market. Taking all these things into consideration I feel that we might agree to this extent, that wre can produce one product which cannot be equalled by any other agricultural country; that is wheat. Whether or not we can produce wheat as cheaply as it can be produced in other countries, due to the difference in standards of living, is a question perhaps not yet decided. Personally I think we can, but even if that is so we still have a big handicap because of our freight rates, both on land and on sea. In butter I think it has been proven that we cannot compete with New Zealand or Australia as far as quality is concerned; for one thing we have not the natural advantages possessed by both these countries, which help them to produce butter so cheaply. However, there is another dairy product which we can produce and sell in the old country markets at a premium; I refer to cheese. So I think if we are to concentrate on dairy products we should concentrate on cheese, and since many think we cannot separate butter and cheese, what assists one is bound to assist the other as well.
As I stated at the outset, in thinking over these problems and discussing them with men especially interested in agriculture, on both sides of this house irrespective of politics, I was confronted with one great question. We have given the Canadian market to the Canadian farmers as far as tariffs have allowed us to do so, but the question is how we can extend the effective range of that tariff. This very small surplus of ten million pounds of butter depressed the price in this country from 28 cents to 17 cents a pound. Is there any way by which that small surplus can be lifted off our market and placed on the old country market? There we are struck with the Patterson scheme of Australia, which I think no one can deny has been a great success. That, however, is not a government measure; it is a matter of voluntary cooperation between certain creameries. In Australia the number of creameries is limited, and it was a comparatively simple matter to get them to cooperate in such a voluntary scheme by which they themselves put a levy of so much on every pound of butter they manufactured. Thus they set up a fund to be used by their export board to absorb a certain amount of the loss on each pound of butter exported. That scheme has worked 41761-176J
very successfully in keeping the price of Australian butter higher than the world price.
The question with which we are faced is how to overcome that difficulty in connection with our agricultural products. With that in mind we did contemplate, and are still contemplating the introduction of a national farm products marketing act. We have fully discussed this matter with hon. members on both sides to see if it would not be possible in some way, by setting up such a board, to work out some scheme-which we thought we had fairly well worked out-to lift this surplus off our market and thus extend the effective range of the protection given by the tariff. However, although I was quite decided in my own mind, in discussing the question with impartial people whose opinions I value highly they pointed out that the Imperial conference, about which so much has been said, taking place in the near future, it might be better to appoint a number of men fully representative of the whole agricultural life of Canada to discuss fully the question I have briefly outlined. There is something to be said for that. Although there might be some benefit in having a board set up before the Imperial conference, on the other hand there would be an advantage in not setting up the board until we have had the benefit of the discussions which will take place here, and until we have seen the effect they may have on our relationships with the other parts of the British Empire.
So far as the dairy industry is concerned, then, we have done this: We have made every effort to improve the quality of the stock that is producing the cream from which our butter is made. We have done everything possible to send out information with regard to the lowering of the cost of production, through experiments in connection with feeding. We have also given to the Canadian farmer the Canadian market. It will be remembered that the dairy industry was discussed last year when my estimates were up, and it was stated then that an impartial and conservative estimate of the value of that Jgeislation was about $12,000,000. I asked my own officers to make an estimate of the value of that legislation, and their figures were somewhat in excess of the amount I have just given. Those who are interested in the dairy industry will realize that during the past few months the very fact that we were able to keep out butter from other countries raised the price of butter in Canada within a very short period to 28 cents per pound, but with the advent of warm weather, production increased about
Supply-Agriculture

20 per cent; we accumulated a visible surplus, and the price dropped to the present level. It is hoped that through the formation of a marketing board some means may be worked out to extend the effective range of our tariff by lifting off the surplus of butter we have in Canada, which has been so detrimental to the price.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if there is an agent in London, England, acting for the Department of Agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: There are trade commissioners in England to act for this and other departments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Is there more than one?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I think there are five or six in all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I heartily approve of the suggestion with regard to a marketing board. I should like to go even further and see our external trade handled entirely by import and export boards. That is coming; sooner or later we will have a condition that will compel us to adopt a policy of that kind. In connection with this marketing board for dairy products I wish to ask the minister if he can give us any idea when it will be set up and what its functions will be.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I thought I had
made it clear that it is not decided yet whether it would be better to bring a marketing board into being at the present time or whether it would be better to wait, in view of the Imperial conference and the many difficulties with which we will be confronted in forming regulations and making this board effective. I am sure no person in the house appreciates better than the hon. member for Bow River the far-reaching results which will follow the setting up of a new board of this kind. Therefore it is felt, though not definitely decided,

that it may be better to appoint men representative of agriculture throughout Canada to make a special study of this question and report before the next session of parliament.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Of course
there can be no objection to the minister getting the best information on the subject that it is possible to get, but his last statement would clearly indicate that there is no intention on his part to appoint such a marketing board at least until the next session of parliament. Frankly I fail to follow his reasoning.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Louder.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen would be quiet they could hear me. I suggest to the minister that his reasoning is not easily followed. I should imagine that because of the coming Imperial conference he would deem it exceedingly advisable to have our marketing, in connection with dairy and other agricultural products, thoroughly organized. He would then have an advantage. At least he would be on an equal basis with several of the other dominions and he would have an advantage over those whose marketing was not organized. I wonder if he would consider that for a moment. I submit that he could enter the Imperial conference m a much stronger position if he had a marketing board.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
That has been and
is being fully considered. One of the questions that doubtless will come up at the Imperial conference is the problem of the various countries putting their goods on the market of the United Kingdom with a bonus, or supported by an artificial levy, and that was one of the advantages which it was felt might come to us by refraining from making the appointment until after the Imperial conference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
What is the
name of the agricultural agent in London.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: There is no agricultural agent in London; I spoke of trade commissioners in the old country. There was an agricultural agent in London, but it was felt that the work would be better coordinated by having, rather than trade commissioners, agricultural agents, and the. different organizations operating with them could all carry on better under one head.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Have they
their offices in London?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
London, Glasgow,
Bristol, Cardiff, Liverpool.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
The minister says he has
had in mind the forming of a marketing board. What will be the functions of the board?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I do not think it would be fair for me to commit myself to a board when we are not yet in a position to decide whether or not such a board shall be appointed or what its powers will be.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I have before me the annual report of the National Dairy Council of Canada, from which I quote the following:
The final result of last season's operations in the butter market is well known. We exported 10,680,000 pounds, chiefly to England. The butter was on the whole well received, and more could have been sold if the offering price had been accepted. Finally we entered the winter season with too much butter on hand, or to put it more accurately, too much to inspire confidence in the market. An effort was made in October and November, to bring about a cooperative export of the assumed surplus. This effort failed, as it was not found possible to induce certain large holders to adhere to it, and the rest would not sacrifice in order to make profits for those who would not take their share of the loss. The market gradually weakened, and in February slipped away to unprecedentedly low levels. The fall at that time was greatly aggravated by banking pressure on certain weak holders who were forced to sell regardless of the market condition. It is questionable whether this policy was wise either from the bankers' standpoint or that of the industry, for it brought about a general lowering of the price level and caused widespread loss and unsettlement.
The question which the foregoing suggests is this:	How will the marketing board be
able to prevent a recurrence of that condition? Would the marketing board be able in some way to lift off the Canadian market the surplus spoken of in that report? If so, how could that be done? The minister must have given a great deal of thought to the subject, and while it is unfair to ask him to state in detail the powers of a. body at present non-existent,. still I am sure a good many members would like to know, how the situation could be met.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
What the hon.
member refers to occurred a little over a year ago. It had been realized that the surplus butter produced in Canada was produced chiefly in the west, and so long as it cannot be removed off the market it will flow into eastern Canada, depressing the price here, and then on to the world market. It was felt, after consideration, that even if the large creameries in the west would agree to make a levy among themselves of half a cent per pound on the butter they manufactured, and
put that into a fund to purchase the butter that was regarded as a surplus in western. Canada, if there were, say, 10,000,000 pounds to export and 225,000,000 pounds produced, one-tenth of a cent per pound on the 225,000-000 pounds produced, distributed over the 10,000,000 pounds, would raise the price of the 10,000,000 pounds in the neighbourhood of 2.25 cents per pound. That, roughly, was the scheme under consideration. The representatives of the different creameries in the west met with me and we went into the matter fully for one or two days, then the conference was adjourned, meeting later in Montreal. Some of the creameries represented had also their own distributing concern in the east, and they thought that they were being called upon to make a contribution that would not net themselves anything. In that they were fair. If, however, it could have been made compulsory, dealing with that incident alone, I have no doubt that the condition that did arise would not have arisen.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
We are now discussing
the present condition of agriculture, and the minister has interjected something with regard to what he proposes to do at some future date, provided certain things happen. I am not concerned with what he proposes to do next year or the year after; I am interested in what he is going to do now. He says that next year, after the Imperial conference, we shall have a marketing board. He, himself, interjects the subject and then he refuses to discuss it because he does not think that it should be discussed prior to the Imperial conference. Well, if we are not going to discuss the marketing board, I should like to know from the minister and from the government what they propose to allow us to discuss in regard to what they have to offer as a means of assisting agriculture in the plight in which it finds itself at the present time. I was very much interested in the talk which the minister has given, if not here, then in some other place. He blames the tariff which has been raised by some other countries against our products going into their markets; he blames other tariffs for preventing us from getting in. But I would point out to the minister that if these countries did this, we retaliated by increasing our tariffs against the imports of other nations, making it that much more difficult for the surplus products of our farms throughout Canada to find markets in the world. Now the minister speaks about the Patterson scheme as it operated in Australia some time ago. I am
Supply-Agriculture

not sure whether it is in operation now, but I know how Canada met it. We met it by applying the dumping duty, so that the butter came into Canada, not at the price at which it was proposed to bring it in, but at the price in the country of origin. If you create a marketing board that operates on the principle laid down in the Patterson scheme, you will find every country applying dumping duties to prevent you doing the very thing which you propose to do. If we are not to have a marketing board this year, let us forget all about it and discuss the problem that is facing us now. Instead of that, the minister says that some day, at some time in the future, we shall have a marketing board; but that is merely a smoke screen in order to enable him to get these estimates through to-night or to-morrow. I remember that in the dying days of last session-in fact it was the last day of the session-when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture came up, we had no opportunity to discuss matters with the minister, and I pointed out to his chief, the Prime Minister, that it was unfair to the minister himself, in the first place, unfair to this house and imfair to the farmers of Canada, that we should be deprived of an opportunity of discussing with the hon. gentleman any proposals he had for the assistance of agriculture. I think it is only fair to him that to-night he should be given an opportunity to say what he will do, not a year or two years from now, but right at this moment. Yesterday I asked the government what they intended to do in connection with the relief measure then under consideration. I was told quite frankly that the government had no policy. Again to-night we find they have no policy; at least none has been enunciated. If the minister, has a policy, I should like to hear him enunciate it and tell us how he proposes to carry it out even with the reduction of thirty-three and a third per cent that is proposed under the estimates at present before the committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I do not think I have anything to add to what I have already said. Our policy is a very definite one. I outlined as clearly" as I could what I thought one of our chief difficulties w^s. It is a matter of judgment whether it would be more advantageous to carry out now the plans that we had suggested, or to have people who are well fitted and representative of agriculture throughout the country to make a special study of the matter' and, if it is thought advisable to do so, have the machinery' ready to appoint this board during next session.

The hon. member has made quite a point of what I have said and what he has read that I have said on different occasions. In that connection I should like to refer to just one statement that the hon. member for South Battleford made earlier in the session, seeing that he has commented on observations that I have made. As reported on page 1363 of Hansard of March 22, 1932, he is reported as saying:
The Minister of Agriculture before the election-he did the same thing after the election - went throughout his constituency and advised some of his followers to hold on to their surplus products because he said prices would soar if the Conservative government were returned to power.
I cannot imagine any statement more devoid of one particle of truth than that made by the hon. member for South Battleford on that particular occasion. When I visited my constituency in January, 1931, one of the times that I have visited it since the last election, I made it perfectly clear to a meeting of my constituents that with the conditions existing in agriculture throughout the world, they had to be prepared to produce bacon at from four to five cents a pound if they were to get a market for it outside of the dominion. In any meetings that I have addressed I have endeavoured to be absolutely fair in any statements I have made regarding agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: In view of what the minister has said, and of the fact that he has nothing further to offer as to how the government proposes to deal with agriculture, with the approval of the committee and in order to expedite matters, I now move that the item of $6,671,100 be passed as the agriculture vote for this year so that the Department of Agriculture may be permitted to carry on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: No; we want to discuss this item by item. It is information we desire. We do not wish to put the minister in a hole. Any questions I have asked have been reasonable, as I think the minister will agree.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I have listened to what the minister has said with regard to the situation in which agriculture finds itself. About a year ago, when he became Minister of Agriculture and before the house met, he had published in several newspapers twelve points that he brought up and what he was going to do for agriculture. I remember referring in the house to those twelve points and telling him what I thought about them.

Supply-A griculture
This year I do not hear him saying anything about them; They have all gone by the board. He has now no policy, and I think my estimate of his policy at that time is just about right. Probably he remembers what my estimate was; I brought it up under point six; it was all answered by number six and that is just what it amounted to. The minister says that the one thing the government has done is to secure the Canadian market for the Canadian farmer. Let me ask the minister: When did the Canadian farmer not have the Canadian market? The trouble was that the Canadian farmer always had the Canadian market, but for many years under Liberal rule they were not able to supply the demands of the Canadian people and some commodities had to be imported. Our farmers at that time did not go in for butter making, chicken raising, egg producing; they went into the most profitable work, that is wheat raising. That was the case until the present government came into power, and then, when conditions went from bad to worse, they had to go into producing eggs and butter, not eating ice cream but making the cream into butter. They did this to try to make a living, and at the present time some of them are making a very poor one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Some hon. members
may laugh, but if to-day they go into western Canada among the farmers and see them in need, they will not be laughing and considering it a joke. This is no laughing matter among the farmers either of western or of eastern Canada, yet when a farm problem is brought before the house, hon. members think they can sit back and laugh.
I understand the minister during the last election campaign told his constituents that they would have to be prepared to produce bacon for four or five cents a pound. Is that the statement he made?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Not during the
election. In January, 1931.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
My information is that
the people who assisted the minister during the last election told his constituents they were going to get big prices for their bacon, eggs and butter. They did not tell the farmers they would have to produce bacon for four or five cents a pound or eggs for four cents a dozen. The other day I received a letter from a man in my constituency saying that the price of eggs in my town was four cents a dozen. He says that it takes a dozen eggs to buy an apple. This is a question in
mathematics: How many dozen eggs would it take to buy a barrel of apples? That is the condition in which the farmers find themselves in western Canada, and yet our farmer friends opposite laugh and think it is a big joke. Even the hon. member for Long Lake thinks it is a laughing matter. I do not know what his constituents will think when he laughs over matters of this kind.
The situation at the present time is very serious and yet the minister has nothing to offer except that he allows the government at such a time as this to cut the estimates. I notice an item for the administration of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act. In to-day's newspapers we are informed the people in western Canada are threatened with an outbreak of pests in the form of cutworms, yet we are told that this estimate is to be cut down this year. We are troubled at this time with pests, and the greatest of them is the present government. That is what is worrying the farmer now, and he is anxious to get out and cast a vote against them. I implore the government to get the best people they possibly can to fight this pest that is threatening the west.
We are told that the Imperial conference is going to do something for ua, and I hope it is. If it is not a success, it will be disastrous for the present government. It is their last sheet anchor, their last hope. We are hoping it will do something for the farmer. I believe the hon. member for South Battleford is quite right: if the government has nothing for agriculture, what is the use of our sitting here and discussing these estimates?
Mr. MALONEY': I agree entirely with my hon. friend from Willow Bunch when he says that the farmer should be given some chance. As I rode to town on the train this morning I saw on either side of the track farmers working strenuously in the fields, .ploughing with the old horses, and they were not thinking .of a five cents a bushel bonus on wheat, or whether they would receive a dollar or a dollar and a half or two dollars a bushel for their wheat; they were satisfied to go on with their work. I thought that showed the spirit of these men, and was a lesson to every citizen of this country. When I listened to the wailings of my hon. friend from Willow Bunch and my hon. friend from South Battleford, and that grand old patriarch the hon. .member for Lis-gar, and remembered what they did not do for the Canadian farmer when they were in a position to do something, it reminded me of an incident which occurred in the state of Minnesota a few years ago. The authorities of that state decided to put on a "save the forest'
