maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Where is it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I would say to -my hon. friends and to the farmers of Canada: Give the present Minister of Agriculture a chance, and he will do something for the farmer, but not with the aid of hon. gentlemen opposite, because they were never known to do anything in 'the line of advancing the interests of the farmer. But the minister will do it, with the aid of the people of Canada, who I believe are absolutely behind him. He will evolve a policy which will be put into effect in this country before many months are over and it will be to the great advantage of the farmers of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend go out and tell the farmers in his constituency that they ought to be satisfied simply to work and not think anything about the prices they get for.their products? That is the kind of farmer he holds up -to us as an example, and that is just the kind of farmer we do not want to see in this -country

farmers satisfied to keep their noses to the grindstone, taking no account of the conditions under which they live, and thinking nothing about the prices they receive for their products.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Not being able to find in the estimates any item covering the salaries of vegetable inspectors and supervisors, I wish to take advantage of the privilege that has been granted to us to discuss agriculture generally to draw the attention of the minister to wha-t I consider to be a grave discrimination in the matter of the dismissal of inspectors and supervisors of vegetables.

I have before me the report on the dismissal of one Conrad Estabrooks, inspector of vegetables, residing at Upper Sackvilde, in the county of Westmorland, New B-runswick. Mr. Conrad Estabrooks was notified- by the department that his services would no longer be required on- account of certain -charges that had been made against him, which charges were investigated without any notification to the accused of the investigation to be held. I have here a copy of a letter signed by R. Weir, dated Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, November 5, 1931, and addressed to R. E. Estabrooks, F, L. Estabrooks & Company, Sackville, N.B., reading as follows:
Dear Sir,-
I am in receipt of your letter of recent date, complaining of our failure to reemploy Mr. D. 0. Estabrooks this fall for potato inspection work.
I have had this matter gone into very carefully by our Mr. Marshall, acting district inspector for the maritime provinces, and our Mr. McIntosh has, I understand, 'written you several letters in this connection.
Mr. Marshall in submitting his report on this case stated, "I find there is a strong feeling in these sections that discrimination has been shown by this inspector. They feel that Inspector Estabrooks

It does not say who feel, but simply "they feel":
-is too young a man to stand the strain of family influence, being closely connected with one of the largest shipping firms in that section."
Under these circumstances -the department felt that there was no option but to decline to have Mr. Estabrooks reappointed this year. It was not a case of his ability as an inspector or otherwise, but rather one of dissatisfaction on the part of shippers coming under the iiispection of this young man, and I feel that the department could not have acted differently in this matter.
Yours very truly,
R. Weir.
This young man asked for the usual investigation and that investigation was refused him. I claim, Mr. Chairman, that where an official is accused of discrimination in the performance of his duty he should if he so desires, be granted an open investigation, and no inspector and no official of the department, or of any department should be sent to hold an ex parte investigation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: The same as you dismissed postmasters.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
My hon. friend had better keep his tongue between his teeth, if he can possibly do so, or I may have a shot or two for him. I claim it was unjust and unfair, Mr. Chairman, to dismiss an official who asked for an investigation and wanted an opportunity to defend himself.

In rising I said I wished to point out unfair discrimination in matters of this kind as practised by the Department of Agriculture. I have before me a case where on the personal certificate of a member of this house a returned soldier was dismissed in 1931. He was a vegetable inspector at the head of his district. After he was dismissed by order in council based on the certificate of the hon. member representing the county-oh, the minister need not make inquiries about the name; I will give it to him before I am through. I shall give him more than a name.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I was not inquiring about the name, but I did think my hon. friend's remarks were somewhat remote from dairying. If the hon. member would wait until the proper time I will have the information he wishes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: There is no use in the minister trying to raise the point of order that we are dealing with dairying. There is no item in his estimates under which I can bring this matter to the attention of the committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Oh yes, there is.
There is a special item for fruit and vegetables.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I claim the same privilege claimed by other members. The minister was granted an opportunity to talk, and I have as many rights in debate as he has.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: A point of order was raised by the hon. member for Melville, and by unanimous consent of the committee it was decided to discuss the whole agricultural policy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
That is what I am doing. Under the personal certificate of the member representing the county, an order in council was passed dismissing the man to whom I refer. The order of dismissal was sent to his chief; his chief notified him; he claimed he was wrongly dismissed, and asked for an investigation under oath. The department notified him that having been dismissed by order in council he could not have an investigation. I agree that when an order in council is passed there is difficulty in recalling it. But what happened in this case? This man, a returned soldier, applied to the soldiers' organization in this city of Ottawa. On his behalf they took the matter up, and after considerable fighting, and pressure brought to bear, the minister notified this man that he would have an investigation, and accordingly an investigation was granted. My point is this: Why
was an investigation granted to a man dismissed by order in council, and refused a man who was dismissed or laid off only by order of the minister? There was no order in council dismissing Estabrooks. I do not know whether we should use the common slang expression, but when the pressure was brought to bear I am wondering whether the minister got cold feet and allowed himself in one case to be influenced by the pressure, but in another case refused an investigation. I should like to go a little further with this latter case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: What was the name?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: The name of the man who was dismissed is Charles D. Smith.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: A brother of ike member?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Not that I know of.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
An investigation took place, and I am going to place on Hansard some of the evidence taken. Mr. Ronald E. Smith was the first witness called, and under oath he testified as follows:
I live at East Florenceville. I am a labourer. I attended a meeting called by the Liberal party at Andover in 1930. That meeting was called by the Liberal party asking Liberal supporters and friends of the Liberal party to attend. I attended the meeting at the request of the Hon. B. F. Smith. He requested me to see what the people at the meeting had to say. It was also for the purpose of seeing what prominent men were there. I saw Charles TK Smith, supervisor of potato inspectors there. 1 was quite near to him. There could be no mistake on my part about his identity. I came back to East Florenceville and reported to Mr. B. F. Smith. I don't know if he took any active part in the meeting.
Later this, man was cross-examined by Mr. Money, the lawyer for the accused Charles D. Smith. Under,cross-examination the witness said:
I am a nephew of the Hon. B. F. Smith. I think it was the morning of the convention that Mr. Smith told me to go there. I live with Hon. B. F. Smith. I drove in. George SmitVs car there that day. He is my cousin and B. F. Smith's son.
Then, when cross-examined ' by Mr. B. F Smith, the member, he went on to reiterate that he saw this man there again. I may say Mr. George E. Smith also swore he saw Mr. Charles D. Smith at Andover on that date.
Now we have the evidence of Mr. Charles D. Smith, the accused:
I live at the parish of Perth, Victoria county. I am the C. D. Smith about whose dismissal this investigation is being held. I was not Jiresent at the convention at Andover as claimed
Supply-Agriculture

by Ronald E. Smith. Since 1919 I have taken no part in politics, other than going to the polls and easting my ballot. from the minister to-night whether he will examine the record to-morrow or later on, and, if he finds what I state to be true: that a charge of discrimination was made; that it was investigated ex parte and that the man was given no opportunity to defend himself, whether the minister will reopen the investigation so as to give this man an opportunity of defending his character.

speechtext:
Discrimination in
duty, which is inefficiency. I have given the matter every consideration that I feel it can be given, but so that there may be no possible doubt as to any unfairness in connection with it, I shall be only too glad to give it further consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
The minister quoted
from a speech which I made in the house on March 22 as follows:
The Minister of Agriculture before the election-he did the same thing after the election - went throughout his constituency and advised some of his followers to hold on to their surplus products because he said prices would soar if the Conservative government were returned to power.
The only thing I am sorry about is that the minister did not read the whole speech and take cognizance of what I said in it. What I was dealing with at that time was the very subject we are dealing with to-night, namely the marketing of the surplus products, not only of western Canada but of the whole dominion. What has the government done in regard to this subject? During the last election campaign they promised the farmers, not only of the west but of the whole country, that if they were elected they would do certain things; they would blast their way into new markets. The present Prime Minister went from one end of the country to the other making those promises to the farmers. What did the government do, not at the special, but at the first regular session of parliament? They sent to the committee on agriculture a certain order of reference asking them to investigate and to report to the house on the marketing problems of Canada. What report did that committee bring in? May I again remind the house that concurrence in that report has never been moved. The closing paragraph of it was as follows:
In view of the situation as it presented itself to the committee it is not considered advisable to make any recommendation. Your committee,
Supply-Agriculture

however, submit that the evidence submitted to it might be usefully studied by members of the house.
That was the only contribution to a solution that was made by this government the first year they were in office. Now, in 1932, what is their suggestion for the relief of agriculture? The minister holds up what I designated before as a smoke screen of something he proposes to do at some future date, but he does not intend to discuss it now. This is what we are interested in; this is why we are trying to object to the thirty-three and a third per cent reduction in the estimates, because we realize it is utterly impossible for this, or, for that matter, any other government to bring about or to attempt to bring about the fulfilment of the promises they gave to the people of Canada during the last election. So I would advise the minister in his spare moments to read the speech that I delivered in this house on March 22 last. The criticism I made then was in the same spirit that actuates me now-I am acting in the very best of faith, hoping to help the minister. I went so far to-night to try to help him as to move that these estimates totalling six million dollars odd be voted now en bloc because of his lack of knowledge as to what he proposed to do with the money, but he would not accept the motion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I listened to what the hon. member for South Renfrew and the hon. member for Marquette said a few moments ago with regard to the Minister of Agriculture. They pleaded with us to give the minister a chance, trying to leave the impression that we were not giving him fair play. The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that for the past two years we on this side of the house and the people of Canada have been giving the minister a chance to carry on and evolve his policy and tell us what he is going to do, but we are still waiting to learn what his policy is, and it is no wonder that we on this side and the people of the country are beginning to lose faith in anything that the minister and this government are going to do for the farmers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Not the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33

I want to say this to

him? All I have to do to show that the people are losing confidence in him is to quote from a farm paper that I have under my hand. Weir, of Saskatchewan, is one of the major di sappointments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Like many other members of the house I have been listening in vain to receive a word of encouragement from the Minister of Agriculture. Some few days ago when we were debating in this house the measure for unemployment and farm relief, I put some questions to the hon. Minister of Labour regarding seed grain and asked him if under that measure farmers who needed it would be allowed to obtain seed grain. I have also written to the hon. Minister of Agriculture with respect to the matter, and I received a reply from him dated May 2, 1932, reading as follows:
There is no appropriation or authority making provision for the purchase or distribution of seed grain to farmers in any province in Canada. This is entirely a provincial responsibility, and I would suggest that you advise your constituent to take this matter up with the municipal authorities or the provincial government, who, I feel sure, will see to it that they are sufficiently provided for.
Yours very truly,
R. Weir.
That answer is not satisfactory to me, Mr. Chairman, nor to the people I represent nor to the people of the province of Quebec. This government is simply passing the buck and saying to the province of Quebec: You do the best you can to help the farmers of your own province. Those members who have been in this house for a number of years know that 41761-177
time and again the farmers of western Canada have received advances and assistance from the federal government in purchasing seed grain when they were in dire necessity. I remember also that not so long ago, about the year 1924, when there was a lack of crop in the district that I represent in this house, the Minister of Agriculture in the government of that day (Mr. Motherwell) found ways and means whereby the people of my county and of the district that was stricken at that time were provided with seed grain in the spring, through the efforts of the federal Department of Agriculture in cooperation with the provincial government. It was due to the services of the seed branch under the direction of Mr. Clark that seed grains were provided for the people in my county The minister now states to me in a letter that there is no way in which the people of the province of Quebec can be helped, when they are in need of seed grain. There is no chance for the people of that province to get assistance from this government, despite the fact that in past years under other governments we were able to obtain help. This evening we were told that- the government has no agricultural policy. I believe that statement is true, and with that in mind I shall keep the minister's letter and show it to the people of my constituency so that everybody may know that the government has no agricultural policy. They may have some thought for their friends in the west, but certainly they care not for the people in the east, and more especially those of the province of Quebec.
While I am on my feet there is another matter to which I should like to draw the attention of the minister. Although we have received promises 'from the present administration, and more especially from the minister whose estimates are under discussion, we find very often that instead of constructive work there is more often destructive work in governmental departments. For instance in the constituency I have the honour to represent within the last six years a gentleman named Paul Langlois had been appointed promoter of sheep and swine raising. This gentleman has done good work, and was retained in office until last year. For no good reason at all, except for reasons of political patronage and advantage, he was promoted to another district on the south shore of the river St. Lawrence. In his place Mr. Latulippe was appointed. Apparently the minister, or his official Mr. MacMillan, claimed that this gentleman had qualifications sufficient to entitle him to succeed Mr. REVISED EDITION
Supply-A griculture

Langlois. What took place was this: For some years previously Mr. Latulippe had been employed by the government of the province of Quebec as promoter of agriculture in the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay. He was dismissed by the provincial legislature because of incompetency, and the fact that he was not able to show satisfactory results in his district. Since this government has taken office, Mr. Latulippe has been given the post of sheep and swine promoter in my constituency.
I have before me a letter from Mr. A. A. MacMillan, chief of the sheep and swine division, addressed to Mr. Edgar Rochette, a member of the Quebec legislature. In that letter Mr. MacMillan states that Mr. Latulippe was highly recommended by officials of the provincial Department of Agriculture, and by other men holding important positions in agricultural circles of the province of Quebec. I have in my hand other letters concerning the appointment of this man. It would appear that Mr. Narcisse Savoie, chief agriculturist in the Quebec Department of Agriculture, wrote Mr. A. A. MacMillan on February 4, 1932, as follows:
As I said in our interview, his presence as sheep and swine promoter in Charlevoix and Montmorency counties is very embarrassing for our men, and we are very perplexed as to the attitude we should adopt towards him. Practically all the parish priests and the majority of the farmers look at him with rather bad dispositions. and we really don't know how good work could be done in such conditions, as a close cooperation between the provincial and the federal employees and the parish priests is necessary to get success.
I should like to know how this government, which is pledged to the promotion and development of agriculture in all parts of Canada, can help the people of Canada to get back on their feet by actions such as I have described. I have received many complaints from the people in my constituency, and they are unanimous in the view that the gentleman who has been appointed by the Civil Service Commission to replace Mr. Langlois will not and cannot make a success of his job because while in the employ of the provincial government he proved a failure.
After Mr. Latulippe left the employ of the provincial government he went into business for himself at Murray Bay. He made a failure of the business, made 'an assignment, and proceedings were taken against him. The appointment of the sheep and swine promoter in the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay was made from a political point of view. During the last election campaign Mr. Latulippe was nothing more than a big drummer, a chief political henchman, carrying all

the big guns and working up public meetings in an election campaign which was notorious throughout the province. The people in Charlevoix-Saguenay cannot be expected to go to that gentleman, meet with him and discuss matters in a fair and legitimate manner when most of them know that during the last election campaign he was their opponent. I have written the minister in this connection and only to-day received a reply telling me that Mr. Langlois had been promoted. He was a worthy official, and I am glad his promotion has become effective. I cannot, however, see any reason for moving him, unless it was to find a job for Mr. Latulippe, who, for reasons I have mentioned should not have been appointed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel
that federal and provincial departments of agriculture and agriculture schools have been stressing production too much. If it has not been true in the past, the fact is to-day that production is not the problem with which agriculture is faced. There is no difficulty in producing sufficient quantities of agricultural products. If the Department of Agriculture is to serve the agricultural industry it must make a sharp swing away from the promotion of production as its chief activity to that of, the cooperative marketing and the processing of farm products. In short, we may say that the business of the Department of Agriculture is to do all it can to meet the economic conditions which the farmer is facing.
At the moment I feel a keen interest in the processing of agricultural products, and I know the minister has been sympathetic concerning the venture about which I am going to speak. In Barrie, Ontario, we have been trying to establish an abattoir for the processing of pork, but we are meeting with very great difficulties. Od/dly enough the banks closed the Barrie abattoir when the overdraft was lower than it had been for some months. The minister well knows the details. I dare say the very close interlocking directorates between banks and abattoirs often makes it impossible for the minister, who himself is sympathetic towards the agriculturist, to do the thing that needs to be done. Is the federal Department of Agriculture considering assistance to experimental stations in processing? It does seem to me that that is exactly what the Barrie station is. The experiment is not being carried on by the government, but by farmers, and they are very hard hit by economic conditions this year. If this plant goes down each producer will sustain a heavy loss. There is no reason

Supply-Agriculture
why it should go down. Yet I do think those farmers stand in great need of a long term loan at a low rate of interest. The minister may say to me that the government is hard pressed for money. In reply, may I say to him that it does seem to me altogether nonsensical to put people back on the land to produce more farm products, for the very fact that at the moment we have more products than can be marketed. I do feel if some of the energy that is being devoted by the government to this back to the land movement was directed to making successful great cooperative ventures and helping these experimental stations in processing, it would be a much sounder agricultural policy. I have no faith at all in the back to the land movement. There is no sense in placing people on the land-people who possibly have very little experience and very little money-while those who have experience and money are being driven off the land. May I again press the minister for some reply in regard not only to the situation of the processing plant in Barrie but to other processing plants which undoubtedly will come out of this present depression. What will be the attitude of the federal government in regard to them?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
The matter has
ibeen given .consideration, but no definite action has been taken yet. It is felt that it is really the work of the provinces rather than of the dominion. For some time we have been discussing with the provinces what assistance could best be given. Similar enterprises have been started, and, I believe, are working out successfully, in the west without any assistance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I am pleased that the hon. member for Chanlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Cas-grain) brought up the question of seed grain, for I am very much interested in it myself. I have received several letters from municipalities in my county asking for seed grain. It is quite true, I believe, that the citizens of the province of Quebec are under the impression that they are not getting at the hands of the government the same treatment as the other provinces are getting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
They are under that impression, rightly or wrongly. I have before me Le Canada of Friday the 6th of May, in which it is stated that last year the Department of Agriculture of Quebec wrote to the federal department asking for aid1 for their farmers, but without success! Undoubtedly several
41761-177 J
members of the provincial government are trying to give the citizens of Quebec the impression that the western provinces are receiving special treatment at the hands of this government. As I wanted to give the parties who wrote me correct information, I went to Mr. Clark, the commissioner of that particular branch, and asked of him if there was a law that applied to the western provinces only. He infonmed me there was none. He added there was a time before the natural resources were transferred to the western provinces when the federal government supplied1 seed grain to the settlers, but since the transfer the western provinces have received no special treatment. He also told me that Quebec and Ontario never took advantage of the law as the western provinces have done, but that the law is the same for all the provinces. He added, "I imagine if asked by Quebec or Ontario to loan money or to guarantee a loan to buy seed grain for the farmers of those two provinces the federal government no doubt would do the same as it is doing for the western provinces, if such action were found necessary." So I should like the Minister of Agriculture, or perhaps the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), to make a clear declaration to the committee so that there will be no more misunderstanding in the province of Quebec with respect ta this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: In connection with seed grain, if any province communicates with the federal government stating that it is not in a position financially to carry on any of its governmental work, the matter is considered and if deemed advisable money is advanced to the province as a loan only, the province being responsible for repayment. The province is responsible for getting seed grain. With regard to the statement that the previous government did give seed grain to the province of Quebec in a very small area, my information is that the provincial government supplied the seed grain, and the federal government increased the subvention that year in connection with it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: The federal government paid for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
As to the criticism with reference to these appointments, one man-evidently he is championed to a certain extent by the hon. member who spoke in connection with sheep grading-the recognition of whose work so far as I know was not disputed as a result was promoted. maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: The minister said there were some experiments in processing that were carrying on successfully in western Canada without loans from the government. Would he say where they are?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: One is in Saskatoon. It was started1 by the Canadian Live Stock Association, and some assistance was given by the government of Saskatchewan. I believe the one at Barrie, to which the hon. member refers, also received assistance from the provincial government of Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: This discussion seems to have gone rather far afield and to have covered a wide range of subjects. I presume we are still on item 39, and I should like to make one or two observations not only with regard to that item but touching some of the other items in the estimates as well. As the representative of a riding which is largely rural I have waited patiently for some statement of policy by the Minister of Agriculture. The chief concern of the farmers in the riding I have the honour to represent appears to be that they also have been waiting for some policy to be brought forward by this government, naturally through the Minister of Agriculture, that would raise their hopes and cheer them up, if nothing more, because the farmers of Ontario are in the same plight as the farmers of western Canada. A few weeks ago I stated in this house that the farmers of Ontario were never in the condition in which they find themselves at present. Not only do they not know how to make ends meet financially; in addition they have lost their morale. They are in the depths of despair, and for almost two years now they have been waiting for some ray of hope.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Twelve years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend
speaking? I have never seen him rise to his feet and speak in this house yet.

speechtext:
You have not been here
yourself.
[Mr. Robert Weir.l

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: He said twelve years, and that is right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I was remarking about the lack of policy of this government especially with reference to agriculture. Most of the letters I have had from my riding have been from farmers asking me when I expected some agricultural policy to be given out by this government. So far this session my reply has been that when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were brought down I hoped the minister would outline some policy which the government might think would be of benefit to the farming communities of the country.
I want to say to the minister that I had a great deal of sympathy with him, and I do not want to be over critical. We realized that the minister came to parliament for the first time after the election of 1930. He was immediately made a minister of the crown, and great hopes were held by his friends that he would at once take hold of the department and endeavour to do something to assist the great basic industry of Canada. I had a great deal of sympathy for him in the special session of 1930 and again last year, because I thought he should be given an opportunity to get well in the saddle before too much criticism was directed at him. I must confess, however, that in this session of 1932, under the conditions existing throughout the country, the sympathy I once had for him has almost vanished. I expected that at least he would rise to-night and give us some sort of policy, but apparently he has no policy at all. The government of the day have no policies on anything; they go on in a hit and miss fashion, and they have not hit very much since they came into power. But it was expected that the Minister of Agriculture, who has been heralded by the Conservative press throughout the length and breadth of this country as one of the outstanding members of this government-

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
My friends across the
way applaud; my hon. friend from South Essex applauds also. I want to tell hon. gentlemen that about all we get from the opposite side is applause. We do not get any policies or any legislation; this government has been just a hit and miss affair ever since it came into power.
To get back to the Minister of Agriculture, I had a great deal of sympathy for him, but now he has been in office for two years; he has brought forward no policy, so he should

Supply-Agriculture
not object if he is subjected to the most severe criticism. Let us consider his statements tonight in connection with item 39, which has to do with dairying. He rather prided himself and rather praised the government on the fact that butter was on an export basis and that a price of 28 cents a pound had been maintained for some time. I would remind the minister and hon. gentlemen opposite that in the campaign of 1930 they went up and down this country, when butter was selling at from 32 to 34 cents a pound, saying "Put in Mr. Bennett and within three weeks the farmers will be getting 70 cents a pound for butter."

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Who said that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: I think my hon. friend from Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said it first, and went up and down the country repeating it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
No; we went up and the
Liberals went down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
The hon. member for
South Essex and the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe cannot stampede me. So I say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not think the government deserve any credit at all in regard to butter. Instead they deserve condemnation, because we must not forget that, led by the right hon. Prime Minister, whose speeches were echoed and reechoed by his lieutenants, hon. gentlemen opposite went about the country saying, "Put us in power and we will get markets for the products of the farm. We will make tariffs fight for the farmer? We will get markets the world over for wheat, butter, bacon, live stock and every other product of the farm." The people of this country have long memories and they have not forgotten, but they have been very patient with the Minister of Agriculture and his department. Now, however, they have come to the point where they have given up all hope of getting anything from this department.
I want to refer for a moment to the debate which took place in this chamber yesterday with regard to Bill No. 72, which was sponsored by the Minister of Labour but which was practically taken out of his hands during the course of the debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: Order. I do not think the hon. gentleman can refer to a previous debate unless it is on the same question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
It is on the same
question. Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
That debate is not yet
concluded.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
According to rule 293
the hon. member may not refer to a previous debate of the same session unless it is on the same question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Bill 72 proposes to give
power to the government to aid in the marketing of farm products.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
That is what I was
going to point out. That bill really is for farm relief and it covers the whole question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
But this is a different
question. The committee is in supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
True, we have been
all over the map to-night from one end of the country to the other. I wrould point out, with all due respect to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, that there is a clause in Bill No. 72 whereby the government seek the power-and by their majority in this house they will get that p0wer-of practically a blank cheque once more to aid any industiy in the country- any manufacturing industry, any bank, any insurance company, any trust company, any corporation, with unlimited credit. They can spend the people's money and are not limited to $1,000,000 but may spend $100,000,000 or $200,000,000. The point I want to make is this-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Order. What the hon.
member has just said convinces me that it is not the same question, and he may not refer to that debate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I do not want to say
much more about it. I have said about ail I wanted to say. The government, under this Bill 72, which will pass in a day or two, will have unlimited power to aid all sorts of manufacturing concerns; yet they come into this house with estimates for the basic industry of Canada and show a reduction in those estimates of $3,300,000 odd, notwithstanding the fact that, if agriculture does not prosper, no one in Canada can be prosperous. They have money for everybody but the farmers. They have money for their friends the big interests; they have money for their friends the manufacturing interests; they have money for everybody except the farmer, and the estimates which should be intended to assist the farmer are reduced by 33J per cent or, as I have pointed out, 83,300,000. As has been pointed out in this house time and again in connection with various matters that have been under discussion, the government seem
Supply-A gricult ure

to forget that the basic industry of this country, namely, agriculture, should receive the first consideration of any administration. But they are going to starve that industry and save millions for the big interests. They will get authority from this house-because they have the majority behind them to carry any measure they bring in-to starve the basic industry of this dominion. They do not appear to be at all concerned about markets for the farmers' products.
Coming back to the minister, he said tonight that he thought he would have a policy. He said, if I heard him rightly, "I discussed the matter with some of my friends and came to the conclusion that there should be a national marketing board. I was of that opinion myself and I still am, but in discussing it with some of my friends I have decided that we will not do anything until after the Imperial conference which is to be held in this city in July." Now, what are they waiting for? Why, three months after they came into power in 1930, if they had been alive to the interests of the country, if they had been alive to our basic industry, they would have formulated some policy for the agriculturists of Canada. But to-day at this late date they have no policy and the minister brings down his estimates to-night, reduced, not by ten per cent but by thirty-three and a third per cent-reduced S3,300,000-and he says, "We have no policy yet, but I have been discussing the question and perhaps after the conference we shall have a policy." Had they been alive to the interests of the farmers, the government would before now have formulated a policy which they could submit to the Imperial conference in an endeavour to obtain a market for the farm products of this country. But they are stifling the trade of the country. They talk about manufacturing in Canada, and hands are being laid off. One thing that the Conservative party has always forgotten is that prosperity in this country must come primarily from the products of the farm. If the farmers are not prosperous, no one will prosper: the manufacturers will have no business, the banks will have no business, the insurance companies will have no business. But hon. gentlemen opposite are neglecting the great basic industry because apparently they do not care. Apparently they do not care for the farmers, but I want to tell them that when the time comes for the farmers of Canada to register their votes, then independent of party feeling or party bias, ninety-five per cent of the Canadian farmers 
will mark their ballots against this government and turn them out, electing some government that will at least realize that the basic industry of Canada is farming.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
We have heard a long
discussion this evening and great anxiety has been expressed by members of the opposition as to what our policy is. I would ask those hon. gentlemen what their agricultural policy was in regard to the dairy industry. They never had a policy; this country simply drifted in that regard. The only legislation which the Liberal government passed, presumably for the benefit of the eastern dairy farmers, was restrictive and it was very injurious to those farmers. We had a hog grading act, an egg grading act, and various inspections. At one time, in 1926, 1927 and 1928, we had four different inspections. We had a Montreal inspection, a provincial inspection, a federal inspection and a New York inspection, with different regulations governing each.
A good deal of anxiety has been expressed in regal'd to our agricultural policy. Let me say that to-day, for the first time in many years, we- have a Minister of Agriculture who exhibits a little bit of sympathy towards mixed and dairy farming. That is something we have not had in this country for many years. I would advise hon. members opposite to have patience for a short time and they will see that distinct, guiding policies will be evolved.
They are complaining about the price of butter to-day. What was it in 1926, 1927 and 1928? We used to compare it with prices in the United States. At the present time we are getting better prices for butter and eggs than farmers in the United States are receiving. In the first fifteen days of September, 1926, the United States farmer got twenty-six cents a pound more for his butter than we did on this side of the line. We got twenty-nine cents while he received fifty-five cents per pound. For twenty years the United States farmers got from seven to twenty cents a pound more than we did. This is the first time in all these years that the price of butter has been higher in Canada than on the other side of the line.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend
seen the last report of the Department of Agriculture under date of May 7 giving comparisons in regard to the price of butter? In Canada it was sixteen and one-half cents while in New York it was twenty and one-half cents.

Supply-Agriculture

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
I do not deny that report
may be correct, but I say, generally speaking for the past six months our egg and butter prices have been much better than they have been across the line.
As regards the reduction in the agriculture estimates and the references made by some lion, members opposite to different inspectors being laid off and so forth, I should like to cite what occurred in the port of Montreal from 1925 to 1930 while the Australian treaty was in force. During that period the then government maintained seventeen butter graders in that port. In 1928 one of them told me that they had hardly enough butter there to grade for their own use and yet seventeen graders were maintained during that time. The peculiar feature about that grading was [DOT]this: When we did happen to have a box or two of butter to export, the Englishmen did not accept our grading; he graded it himself. My hon. friends opposite have been making loud noises just to impress their electors; that is all they are doing. I agree with many of them that agriculture is very important and I maintain that the dairy farmer of the east is entitled to some consideration. I have nothing tp say against the wheat growers, but for the last fifteen or twenty years, what attention has been devoted to agriculture has been for the benefit of the grain growers of the west. They must not forget that for one grain grower west of the lakes there are two farmers in the east, and that seventy-five per cent of the taxes come from Ontario and Quebec. We want to do anything we can to help the grain growers, but I submit that the whole agricultural policy of the government should not be for the benefit of the west.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: After such a speech, the farmers of the eastern townships will be prosperous and rich. I have never before heard a member representing a rural constituency uttering such nonsense as the hon. gentleman has done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext: To say that an hon. member is talking nonsense is hardly parliamentary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-WHEAT BONUS CONTINUATION OF PAYMENT OF FIVE CENTS A BUSHEL ON CHOP 1932-33
speechtext:
Well, I will say not common sense. My hon. friend spoke against inspectors. There are inspectors to classify daily products, indeed, to classify all farm products, and it is only after such a classification that the farmers can get a fair price. This is something that is known to every man, even to a doctor who lives among farmers. I have for a long time advocated the appointment of inspectors for farm products, because such inspection is most essential. Formerly farm
products and, in particular, potatoes, were not graded and the farmers got very little for their products. After inspectors were appointed, after farm products were graded, the farmers received much higher prices. The reason why inspectors should be appointed is that farm products may be graded one, two, three, or A, B, C, as the case may be, so that when the purchaser goes to the market he can get exactly what he wants, for instance, grade 1 or grade 2 potatoes and so on. In the old days that was not the case. When the hon. member for Brome-iMissisquoi was young, when a man went into a store and asked for something, he would be told by the merchant: I have not that, but you should take this and it will suit you just as well. Well, when a purchaser goes to a store and says he wants such and such, if he does not get it, he goes to the next store or to the next town in order to get it.
I must congratulate the hon. member for Missisquoi on rising to speak. We have all heard about the Tories from Quebec being dead. I might use in respect to them the term which was used during the war "debout les morts"-"Stand up, you dead." Since the election took place we have not heard fiom them in regard to butter. They have been as silent as rocks. I cannot compare them to trees, because sap comes out of trees. They are just as dumb as stones. Now they swallow what they vomited before the election. This is what all the Tories from the province of Quebec, especially those from the eastern townships, who were elected because of butter, have been doing. During the last election we heard all sorts of, not nonsense, but things that were not common sense. I make an exception to you, Mr. Chairman, because I have more consideration for you than for your colleagues in the party from Quebec.
Progress reported.
